strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: preserving watermarks when 3D Gaussian Splatting models undergo compression. Integrating watermarking with anchor-based representations is a useful direction.

Table 1 reports promising compression robustness across two backbones: HAC bit accuracy remains 95.95% to 95.92%, while ContextGS retains 94.03% after compression, with minimal rendering-quality degradation and compact model sizes.

Evaluation covers 25 scenes across three datasets, multiple image and model perturbations, and three payload lengths. The quantization-layer ablation provides concrete evidence of benefit, improving post-compression accuracy from 90.75% to 95.92% and PSNR from 26.75 to 27.65.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. Existing methods are adapted to anchor-based representations, but implementation and tuning details are insufficient. The paper acknowledges that these adaptations break HAC compression assumptions and make 3D-GSW pruning remove entire anchors, producing severe quality degradation. Comparisons against compression-aware versions of these baselines, especially WateRF with the same quantization simulation, are needed to establish superiority beyond correcting this incompatibility.

The novelty of the principal components is limited or insufficiently demonstrated. Uniform-noise quantization simulation is adopted from existing compression methods, and low-frequency decoding follows WateRF. Since both f and f' are optimized, f + tanh(f') is an overparameterization of the anchor feature; no direct-feature-optimization control establishes why this additional parameterization is necessary.

The frequency-aware growing claims conflict with the quantitative ablation. In Table 5, adding FAG increases bit accuracy but reduces PSNR from 27.75 to 27.64 and SSIM from 0.855 to 0.851, with unchanged LPIPS. Removing all three components also lowers, rather than improves, bit accuracy relative to the full method. These results do not support the accompanying claims of consistently improved image quality or severe degradation without the components.

The frequency-selection mechanism needs stronger technical justification. Equation 8 suppresses a ring at distance tau rather than necessarily suppressing the lowest frequencies when tau is nonzero. Selecting errors near the median in Equation 9 also does not inherently identify high-frequency regions or regions most needing refinement. Values for tau and beta, selection visualizations, and comparisons against ordinary or error-based growing are missing.

Compression efficiency is not convincingly isolated. There is no unwatermarked HAC/ContextGS reference, matched-rate comparison, or rate–distortion–watermark tradeoff curve. Equation 12 contains no explicit rate objective despite a learnable quantization step that can approach zero; the relationship between training noise, entropy-model optimization, and actual encoded quantization is insufficiently specified.

Copyright-identification claims exceed the evaluation. Average bit accuracy does not establish reliable ownership verification without false-positive rates, detection thresholds, unwatermarked controls, or message-level recovery results. Model-perturbation and payload-length experiments are performed before compression, leaving their interaction with the paper's central deployment setting untested.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. The supplied manuscript lacks the referenced supplementary details, training schedules, decoder-pretraining protocol, repeated-run uncertainty, and per-scene results. Table 2 specifies image-noise sigma=0.1 while the text gives 0.005; Table 7 is labeled HAC while its discussion identifies ContextGS. These ambiguities weaken confidence in otherwise promising aggregate results.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical problem: preserving 3D Gaussian Splatting watermarks through compression while retaining rendering quality.
Table 1 reports promising results with two compression backbones. With HAC, watermark accuracy remains approximately 95.9% after compression, while PSNR changes only from 27.68 to 27.65 dB.

Evaluation covers 25 scenes across three datasets, multiple message lengths, and several image and model distortions. The quantization-layer ablation provides positive evidence, improving post-compression accuracy from 90.75% to 95.92%.
weaknesses: Baseline fairness is insufficiently established. The paper adapts existing methods to anchor-based representations but provides little implementation detail. HAC baselines collapse to roughly 13 dB after compression, and 3D-GSW already achieves only about 19.5 dB beforehand. The authors acknowledge incompatibilities involving quantization, entropy coding, and pruning. These comparisons do not isolate the proposed contribution from baseline adaptation failures; compression-aware versions of the baselines are needed.

The central compression claim lacks a controlled rate–distortion evaluation. There are no unwatermarked HAC/ContextGS references, matched-storage comparisons, or sweeps over compression strengths. Consequently, the watermark's incremental quality and storage costs remain unclear. Training and rendering overheads are also absent despite claims of efficiency.

Novelty beyond integrating existing techniques is limited and insufficiently isolated. Quantization-noise training is adopted from compression methods, and low-frequency decoding follows WateRF. The learnable additive feature is not compared against directly optimizing anchor features with the same watermark objective. Since both feature terms are optimized, its distinct benefit requires evidence.

The frequency-aware growing claim is contradicted by the aggregate ablation. Adding FAG in Table 5 improves bit accuracy but reduces PSNR from 27.75 to 27.64 and SSIM from 0.855 to 0.851, with unchanged LPIPS. This does not support the stated improvement in both fidelity and accuracy. The table also uses cumulative configurations rather than independently removing every component.

Important methodological details remain unresolved. Equation 8 is not generally a monotonic high-pass mask for nonzero cutoff, and selecting errors near the median is not justified as identifying high-frequency regions needing refinement. The learnable quantization step can approach zero, yet Equation 12 specifies no rate penalty or other mechanism preventing this; its relationship to the actual codec objective needs clarification.

Copyright identification is evaluated only through average bit accuracy. There are no false-positive rates, detection thresholds, unwatermarked controls, or message-level recovery results. Model attacks and payload experiments are reported before compression, leaving their interaction with the deployed compressed representation untested. Attack severity sweeps and resulting rendering quality are also missing.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. The supplied manuscript lacks decoder pretraining details, training schedules, several mask parameters, and variability across messages or runs. Table 7 identifies HAC in its caption but ContextGS in the text; image-noise strength differs between Table 2 and the prose. These issues, together with the evaluation gaps, leave the evidence below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: retaining watermarks when 3D Gaussian Splatting models undergo compression.

Reports promising results across 25 scenes and two compression frameworks. In Table 1, CompMarkGS retains 95.92% bit accuracy after HAC compression and 94.03% after ContextGS compression, with little rendering-quality degradation.
Evaluates multiple image distortions, model perturbations, and message lengths. Table 7 provides positive evidence that quantization-aware training improves post-compression watermark recovery.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons do not adequately isolate the contribution. Existing methods are adapted to anchor representations, with acknowledged incompatibilities: 3D-GSW pruning damages entire anchors, and HAC baselines lose substantial rendering quality after compression, falling to roughly 13 dB PSNR. Comparisons against carefully adapted, quantization-aware baselines are needed to distinguish methodological gains from integration failures.

The compression claim lacks essential controls. There are no unwatermarked HAC/ContextGS results, matched-rate comparisons, or rate–distortion–watermark curves. Consequently, the watermark's storage and fidelity overhead and the claimed compression advantage remain unclear.

Novelty is insufficiently established beyond combining existing techniques. Uniform-noise quantization simulation is inherited from compression methods, and low-frequency decoding follows WateRF. There is no comparison against directly optimizing anchor features to establish the benefit of the additive learnable embedding.

The ablation interpretation contradicts Table 5. Adding frequency-aware growing changes PSNR from 27.75 to 27.64 and SSIM from 0.855 to 0.851, despite claims that it improves both. Removing all components yields 94.68% accuracy versus 95.16% for the full method, contradicting the stated accuracy improvement. The table also does not independently ablate every component.

The frequency-selection mechanism needs stronger justification. Equation 8 does not generally suppress the frequency origin when its cutoff parameter is nonzero, and selecting errors near their median does not establish that selected pixels contain high-frequency detail. Neither choice is adequately validated.

Copyright-identification claims exceed the evaluation. Average bit accuracy is reported without false-positive rates, detection thresholds, exact-message recovery, or variation across messages and runs. Model attacks and message-length experiments are evaluated before compression, leaving their interaction with the central deployment setting untested.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the supplied manuscript: baseline adaptation procedures, decoder pretraining, optimization schedules, and several frequency-mask settings are missing. Reporting inconsistencies include image-noise strength differing between text and Table 2, and Table 7 being labeled HAC while its discussion identifies ContextGS.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: preserving ownership watermarks when 3D Gaussian Splatting assets undergo compression. Integrating watermarking with anchor-based representations is a sensible direction.

Reports strong compression retention across 25 scenes and two compression frameworks. In Table 1, CompMarkGS retains 95.92% bit accuracy under HAC and 94.03% under ContextGS, with only approximately 0.03–0.05 dB PSNR degradation after compression.

The evaluation is reasonably broad, including image and model distortions, multiple message lengths, compression-level curves, and supplementary experiments with INT8 quantization, pruning, an alternative decoder, and adversarial perturbations.

Component ablations provide positive evidence for the proposed combination. Removing QDL consistently reduces post-compression bit accuracy, while the feature-embedding and anchor-growing experiments support the chosen design.
weaknesses: Baseline fairness is a major unresolved concern. All competitors are adapted to an anchor-based architecture, including replacing GuardSplat's central SH embedding mechanism with feature offsets. Several adaptations already perform poorly before compression: GuardSplat achieves only 16–17 dB PSNR and 3D-GSW approximately 19.5 dB. CompMarkGS also trains from scratch, whereas the competing approaches normally fine-tune existing models. Matched training budgets, stronger adaptation validation, and comparisons within the baselines' native representations are needed to establish superiority.

The strongest simple baselines are missing. QDL explicitly repurposes an existing quantization-noise mechanism, while frequency-domain decoding and distortion-aware watermark training are established techniques. Applying the same quantization augmentation to a competitive anchor-feature watermark baseline would help establish the contribution beyond standard quantization-aware training. Unwatermarked HAC/ContextGS references are also needed to quantify the actual fidelity and storage cost of watermarking.

The central quantization mechanism is underspecified. Equation 4 predicts a learnable noise scale that can approach zero, but the stated objective contains no explicit rate term or constraint preventing the predictor from reducing the training distortion. The paper does not sufficiently explain whether this predictor is fixed, jointly optimized, or shared with the deployed compressor, nor establish correspondence between simulated noise and actual quantization settings.

Several technical explanations are not supported by the definitions. For nonzero cutoff, the purported high-pass filter in Equation 10 suppresses a ring at that cutoff and need not suppress DC. Selecting errors near the median does not necessarily identify poorly reconstructed high-frequency regions. The HSV loss appears to be hue-masked image MSE rather than a perceptual distance in HSV. These issues weaken the claimed mechanisms despite favorable aggregate ablations.

Ownership verification is evaluated mainly through average bit accuracy. There are no false-positive measurements on unwatermarked assets, detection thresholds, message-level recovery rates, or variability across independently sampled messages and training seeds. The claim that implicit MLPs provide strong security is not established by obscuring explicit Gaussian attributes. The supplementary PGD experiment helps, but omits attack norm, iteration count, step size, and resulting image quality, limiting its evidential value.

Reproducibility and reporting require improvement. The compression setting described as a 'ratio' of 0.004 is insufficiently specified; detailed compressor adaptation, quantization calibration, and training-time costs are missing. Some results need reconciliation: Table 8 describes pruning already compressed models yet reports pre-pruning sizes far above Table 1's compressed sizes, and Table 13 reports HAC GaussianMarker accuracy increasing from 58.34% without distortion to 87.89% after pruning without explanation. These ambiguities materially reduce confidence in the compression evaluation.

strengths: Addresses a relevant practical problem: preserving watermarks when 3D Gaussian Splatting assets undergo quantization-based compression.
Reports promising joint fidelity and robustness: Table 1 shows post-compression bit accuracies of 95.92% for HAC and 94.03% for ContextGS, with approximately 27.6 dB PSNR and compact model sizes.

The evaluation covers 25 scenes, two compression frameworks, multiple message lengths, image/model distortions, and component ablations. Supplementary experiments include another decoder, general int8 quantization, pruning, and compression-level sweeps.
weaknesses: Baseline fairness is a major unresolved issue. All competing methods are adapted to an anchor-based representation, including replacing GuardSplat's central SH mechanism with anchor-feature offsets. GuardSplat and 3D-GSW already have poor pre-compression PSNR, while HAC reduces other baselines to approximately 13 dB. These comparisons conflate watermark robustness with architectural adaptation and reconstruction failure. Native-representation comparisons and baselines receiving equivalent compression-aware training are needed.

The central QDL mechanism is insufficiently specified. Equation 4 learns a noise scale that can approach zero, but the stated objective provides no explicit constraint or rate penalty preventing that outcome. The paper does not clarify whether the scale predictor is frozen, how it relates to the deployed quantizer, or whether training targets the same compressor used for evaluation. Learned-scale statistics and fixed-noise or straight-through quantization controls would help substantiate the mechanism.

Ownership verification is evaluated almost entirely through average bit accuracy. There are no false-positive measurements on unwatermarked assets, detection thresholds, true-positive rates at controlled false-positive rates, or message-level recovery results across independently sampled messages. Consequently, the experiments do not establish reliable ownership identification.

The frequency-aware growing formulation does not fully support its interpretation. Equation 10 suppresses frequencies around radius tau rather than generally suppressing low frequencies, unless tau is zero; its parameter settings are not supplied. Selecting errors near the median also need not identify high-frequency regions with poor reconstruction. These choices require clarification and controlled comparisons with conventional growing at matched anchor counts.

The methodological novelty is primarily an integration of existing ideas: anchor features, additive embedding, quantization-noise augmentation, frequency-guided densification, and color masking. Table 5 supports the usefulness of the combination, but comparisons against simpler compression-aware watermarking variants are missing. The explanation that additive features decouple scene representation and watermarking is also stronger than the evidence, since both enter the same summed feature.

Security claims exceed the demonstrated threat model. An implicit MLP does not itself establish resistance to watermark discovery or removal when model parameters are accessible. The supplementary PGD test is useful, but reports only an epsilon value without attack iterations, step size, restarts, or resulting image quality, preventing a convincing assessment of adaptive robustness.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting remain incomplete. The paper lacks repeated-run variability and detailed per-scene quantitative results, does not establish the fidelity cost relative to an unwatermarked model under the same training/compression pipeline, and leaves baseline optimization budgets and several compression details unclear. These gaps materially weaken confidence in the reported margins.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical problem: preserving 3DGS watermarks when assets are compressed for distribution. Integrating watermarking with anchor-based representations is well motivated.

Reported compression results are promising. Table 1 shows bit accuracy changing only from 95.95% to 95.92% under HAC and from 94.36% to 94.03% under ContextGS, with minimal rendering-quality degradation.

The evaluation covers 25 scenes, two principal compression methods, multiple payload lengths, and image/model distortions. The appendix adds compression-level curves, INT8 quantization, pruning, an alternative decoder, and rendering-speed measurements.
Component ablations support the usefulness of quantization-aware training, feature-space embedding, frequency-aware growing, and the color loss within the proposed pipeline.
weaknesses: Baseline fairness is a major unresolved concern. All competitors are transferred to an anchor-based architecture, including replacing GuardSplat’s central SH mechanism with feature offsets. Several adaptations already have very poor fidelity before compression, and HAC subsequently collapses baseline PSNR to approximately 12–14 dB. This makes watermark failure difficult to distinguish from failure of the adapted reconstruction/compression pipeline. Strong, validated adaptations with comparable training budgets and a baseline augmented with the same quantization noise are needed.

The central technical novelty is limited: QDL repurposes established uniform-noise quantization simulation, while low-frequency decoding and frequency-guided densification build on existing watermarking approaches. The experiments do not establish how much benefit requires the proposed design beyond adding standard quantization-aware training to a competent anchor-based watermarking baseline.

The QDL specification leaves a consequential optimization ambiguity. Equation 4 predicts a trainable noise scale that can approach zero, but Equation 9 contains no explicit rate objective or constraint preventing this. The paper should clarify whether the quantization predictor is frozen, jointly optimized with an inherited compression objective, or otherwise constrained, and how training noise corresponds to inference quantization.

Some methodological explanations do not follow from the equations. Selecting errors near the median does not necessarily identify poorly reconstructed high-frequency regions. Equation 10 is not generally a high-pass filter for a nonzero cutoff, since it suppresses a ring around the cutoff and can retain DC. The claimed HSV-space loss also appears to be hue-masked image MSE rather than an explicitly defined HSV-space distance. These issues weaken reproducibility and the proposed mechanisms’ justification.

Copyright-verification and security claims exceed the evaluation. Mean bit accuracy alone does not establish reliable ownership detection: false-positive rates on unwatermarked assets, detection thresholds, message-level recovery, and variability across messages are absent. The PGD experiment is useful but omits essential attack settings such as step count, step size, and objective; nonlinear MLP processing alone does not substantiate resistance to watermark removal.

Important controls and reporting details are missing. There is no unwatermarked HAC/ContextGS reference to isolate watermark-induced quality and storage costs, no uncertainty across training seeds/messages, and no embedding-time comparison despite training from scratch. Some supplementary results also require reconciliation: Table 8 describes pruning already-compressed models but reports pre-pruning sizes far above Table 1, and Table 13 reports HAC GaussianMarker accuracy increasing from 58.34% to 87.89% after pruning without explanation.
